prompt.context: Your client is Whitesand Capital Partners, a large asset manager based in the US with $5 Trillion in Assets Under Management (AUM) and a presence in all large financial centers around the world. Whitesand was known for having some of the best talent in managing fixed income (bond) products in the past, and are continuingly expanding their product offerings to clients by acquiring a number of other asset managers with different strengths. Despite AUM growth in both of their customer segments, Retail and Institutional, and being the largest asset manager in the world, Whitesand has recently been facing declining profitability and shareholders are demanding a shift in strategy.
prompt.question: The CEO of Whitesand has brought you in to diagnose the problems, and to help turn the firm's share price around. How would you approach this?

clarifying_info.q: What is the goal / target for improvement?
clarifying_info.a: The goal is simply to improve profitability; there is no specific number in mind.

clarifying_info.q: How does the company generate revenue?
clarifying_info.a: The company generates revenue by charging a fee on AUM managed. Example: 1% on $1 Million AUM = $10,000 in revenue.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the customer segments and how are they split?
clarifying_info.a: The two main customer segments are Retail and Institutional. Retail AUM and Institutional AUM are split 50/50, but the Institutional segment is growing faster.

clarifying_info.q: What kinds of products do Retail and Institutional investors use?
clarifying_info.a: Retail investors invest in simpler products like stocks and bonds. Institutional investors can invest in any kind of product.

exhibits.title: Asset Class Expense Ratio (Basis Points, 1/100th of a Percent)
exhibits.shows: Bar chart showing the expense ratios (in basis points) for eight asset classes across three years: 2016, 2018, and 2020. The asset classes are: US Equity Active, US Equity Passive, US Fixed Income Active, US Fixed Income Passive, International Equity Active, International Equity Passive, International Fixed Income Active, and International Fixed Income Passive.
exhibits.data: Y-axis: 0 to 140 basis points. Three year bars per asset class (2016, 2018, 2020). Active products have higher expense ratios than passive products. All expense ratios show a declining trend from 2016 to 2020 across all eight asset classes.

exhibits.title: Private Equity Index Returns (Yearly, %)
exhibits.shows: Bar chart showing yearly returns (%) for four types of Private Equity funds across three years: 2016, 2018, and 2020. The fee formula is also shown: Total Fees = Management Fee * AUM + Performance Fee * AUM * (Return - Hurdle Rate).
exhibits.data: Leveraged Buyout: 13% (2016), 15% (2018), 14% (2020). Distressed Debt: 11% (2016), 9% (2018), 17% (2020). Growth: 13% (2016), 11% (2018), 14% (2020). Venture Capital: 23% (2016), 6% (2018), 14% (2020). Y-axis: 0 to 25%. Fee formula shown: Total Fees = Management Fee * AUM + Performance Fee * AUM * (Return - Hurdle Rate).

framework: Revenue: Fee rates (expense ratios / basis points) charged on AUM across product types and customer segments
Revenue: AUM growth or decline by segment (Retail vs Institutional) and product type (Active vs Passive, Equity vs Fixed Income)
Costs: Fixed costs (headcount, technology, real estate)
Costs: Variable costs (trading, sourcing, fund operations)
Investors: Retail vs Institutional preferences and growth trajectories
Products: Current product mix and competitive positioning vs peers
Competitive landscape: Fee compression trends across the industry
Market opportunity: New higher-fee product categories (e.g., Private Equity / Alternatives)
M&A history: How well have prior acquisitions performed? Could further acquisitions accelerate entry into new segments?

questions.prompt: After reviewing Exhibit 1, what are the key insights and what does this mean for Whitesand?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify: (1) Expense ratios (fees) are declining across ALL eight asset classes from 2016 to 2020 — this is fee compression. (2) Active products charge higher fees than passive products. (3) Returns between passive and active classes are roughly the same, so money is flowing from higher-fee active products to lower-fee passive products. (4) This explains declining revenue despite AUM growth. (5) A strong candidate will note that the Retail segment has a stronger appetite for lower-fee passive products, while Institutional investors are more willing to pay higher fees for potentially higher returns — and will ask whether there is a way to target Institutional clients with new, higher-returning products.

questions.prompt: What could Whitesand do to reverse the profitability trend?
questions.guidance: Candidate should move toward higher-fee or higher-yielding products. Ideal direction: new products with higher fees that target the growing Institutional segment. The interviewer should steer toward Private Equity as the answer if not raised spontaneously. Other acceptable answers include marketing active products more aggressively or acquiring a firm with a differentiated product.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, calculate the total fees Whitesand would earn per fund type, assuming Private Equity uses a 2/20 fee model (2% management fee on capital invested, 20% performance fee on returns above a 7% hurdle rate) and $3 Billion in invested capital per fund. Use the three data points to extrapolate an average return for each fund type.
questions.guidance: Candidate should average the three years of returns for each fund type to get a representative return, then apply the 2/20 model. The fund with the highest total fees is the most attractive on a pure fee basis, but the candidate should also discuss qualitative factors.

math.setup: For each fund: Average Return = (2016 + 2018 + 2020) / 3. Management Fee = $3B * 2%. Variable Fee = $3B * (Avg Return - 7%) * 20%. Total Fees = Management Fee + Variable Fee.
steps: Leveraged Buyout avg return = (13+15+14)/3 = 14%. Mgmt Fee = $3B * 2% = $60M. Variable Fee = $3B * (14%-7%) * 20% = $3B * 7% * 20% = $42M. Total = $102M.
Distressed Debt avg return = (11+9+17)/3 = 12.3%. Mgmt Fee = $60M. Variable Fee = $3B * (12.3%-7%) * 20% = $3B * 5.3% * 20% = $31.8M. Total = $91.8M.
Venture Capital avg return = (23+6+14)/3 = 14.3%. Mgmt Fee = $60M. Variable Fee = $3B * (14.3%-7%) * 20% = $3B * 7.3% * 20% = $43.8M. Total = $103.8M.
math.answer: Venture Capital: $103.8M > Leveraged Buyout: $102M > Growth: $93.6M > Distressed Debt: $91.8M. Venture Capital generates the highest total fees.

questions.prompt: Beyond fee calculations, what other factors should Whitesand consider when deciding which type of Private Equity fund to launch?
questions.guidance: Strong answers include: (1) Volatility of returns — Venture Capital has very high return variance (6% to 23%), which means variable/performance fees could be zero in bad years. (2) Fund size and capital requirements. (3) Start-up costs: talent acquisition or firm acquisition needed. (4) Competition in each PE segment. (5) Investor asset allocation constraints — Institutional investors may have limits on how much they can allocate to each PE type. (6) Fit with Whitesand's brand and existing capabilities (historically strong in fixed income, not in VC).

brainstorming.prompt: What qualitative factors should Whitesand consider when evaluating which Private Equity fund type to launch?

categories.name: Return Volatility & Fee Risk
ideas: Venture Capital has the highest average return but extreme variance (6%–23%); in a down year variable fees may be zero
Leveraged Buyout has tighter return band (13%–15%), making fee revenue more predictable
Distressed Debt had one exceptional year (17%) but lower average

categories.name: Start-up & Operational Costs
ideas: Talent is scarce and expensive in Private Equity; may need to hire or acquire a team
Whitesand could acquire a PE boutique to gain instant capability and track record
Each PE type requires different expertise (VC = startup due diligence; LBO = leveraged finance; Distressed = credit restructuring)

categories.name: Market & Competition
ideas: LBO and Growth are crowded segments with many established players
VC is competitive but Whitesand brand may attract institutional LP capital
Distressed Debt is countercyclical and may align with Whitesand's fixed income heritage

categories.name: Institutional Investor Demand
ideas: Institutional clients are growing faster and can invest in PE; natural captive distribution
Asset allocation policies at pension funds and endowments may limit PE concentration
Existing institutional relationships lower distribution costs for a new PE product

categories.name: Brand & Strategic Fit
ideas: Whitesand is known for fixed income; Distressed Debt may be the most natural extension
VC is a stretch from the current brand but offers highest fee upside
Entering PE via acquisition preserves track record requirements many institutional LPs demand

recommendation: Whitesand Capital Partners should enter the Private Equity market to restore profitability and shareholder confidence.
On pure fee economics, Venture Capital and Leveraged Buyout are the most attractive fund types at ~$103.8M and ~$102M in fees per $3B invested.
Given return volatility and brand fit, Leveraged Buyout is likely the more defensible entry point, with Venture Capital as a longer-term option once a track record is established.
risks: Venture Capital return volatility could result in zero performance fees in down years, making revenue unpredictable.
Start-up costs (talent, technology, brand building) for a new PE platform are significant and could further pressure near-term profitability.
Traditional active/passive products will likely continue to see fee compression, so PE entry is a shift in strategy, not a supplement to the status quo.
Institutional investors may already be heavily allocated to PE, limiting the incremental addressable market.
Entering a competitive PE market without an existing track record may make fundraising difficult.
next_steps: Conduct a deeper competitive analysis of each PE segment to identify where Whitesand can differentiate.
Assess M&A targets: identify PE boutiques that could be acquired to fast-track entry and provide a track record.
Survey existing Institutional clients to gauge appetite and capacity for PE allocation.
Model out start-up investment required and time to breakeven for a new PE platform.
Evaluate whether Distressed Debt offers a lower-cost entry given Whitesand's existing fixed income expertise.
